editorNote: Moonshot AI beat its own deadline, dropping Kimi K3's open weights on Hugging Face a day early. Elsewhere, a federal prosecution over a GrapheneOS phone wipe raises the odd legal question of whether using a privacy feature can itself count as evidence destruction, an LLM knocked out formal proofs for a compression algorithm's core routine in the time it takes to get coffee, and Vercel shipped a TypeScript compiler that skips the JavaScript engine entirely.

stories.headline: Kimi K3's open weights land on Hugging Face, a day ahead of schedule
stories.summary: Moonshot AI published open weights for Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter model it bills as the first open '3T-class' model — on Hugging Face around 7:30pm EDT on July 26, a day ahead of the July 27 target it had set when the hosted version launched on July 16. Moonshot's self-reported benchmarks put K3 ahead of Claude Opus 4.8 Max and GPT-5.5 High but behind Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol; independent evaluator Artificial Analysis measured its Elo at 1547, a 732-point jump over Kimi K2.6 and second only to Claude Fable 5.
stories.whyItMatters: Open weights give developers unrestricted access to what Moonshot calls the largest openly released model to date, rather than only a hosted API.

sourceLinks.title: Kimi K3, and what we can still learn from the pelican benchmark (Simon Willison)

stories.headline: Atlanta man charged after his GrapheneOS phone wiped itself during an airport search
stories.summary: The US Department of Justice charged Sam Tunick under a federal statute against destroying property to prevent its seizure, after his phone appeared to wipe itself when he was pressured to unlock it during secondary screening at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta airport on January 24, 2025, amid questioning about suspected ties to anti-Cop City activism. GrapheneOS's passcode-triggered wipe is a built-in privacy feature; his defense says the search violated his constitutional rights and that the wipe may have triggered automatically, while prosecutors treat it as intentional evidence destruction. A ruling is expected by late October.
stories.whyItMatters: Charging the use of a phone's own built-in security feature as evidence destruction is a legal theory security researchers warn could effectively criminalize privacy tools themselves.

sourceLinks.title: US prosecutors charge Atlanta man after GrapheneOS phone wipes during airport search (TechSpot)

stories.headline: An LLM wrote formal proofs for a Zstandard decompressor's core algorithm in about 20 minutes
stories.summary: A developer built a Zstandard decompressor in the Lean proof language, then had LLMs automatically generate formal proofs of universal properties of its Finite State Entropy table construction — including correct table size, a probability-weighted state distribution, and valid state transitions — in about 20 minutes, using only a fraction of a $20/month subscription's quota. The author contrasts this with the seL4 project's finding that proving subtle invariants took roughly 10 times the effort of writing the code itself.
stories.whyItMatters: If LLMs can now automate the proof-engineering effort that made dependent types impractical for everyday software, formally verified invariants could become a routine part of engineering instead of a specialist's undertaking.

stories.headline: Vercel's Scriptc compiles TypeScript straight to native binaries with no JS engine inside
stories.summary: Scriptc runs TypeScript through the real TypeScript compiler's parser and type-checker into a typed intermediate representation, then to C or LLVM and native code via clang, producing static binaries of about 170-200KB that start in roughly 2.4ms and use 1-4MB of memory, versus about 47ms startup and 67-116MB for Node. Code that can't compile statically falls back to an embedded ~620KB QuickJS engine rather than failing silently, and the project claims byte-for-byte compatibility with Node's behavior, verified through differential testing against more than 800 test programs.
stories.whyItMatters: It's a concrete attempt to give TypeScript the small, fast-starting binaries associated with compiled languages without giving up Node API compatibility.
